\chapter{Big, and How an Adjective Agrees}
\label{ch:mr-the-adjective}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can call a thing big in all three genders, and I can say where a Marathi adjective stands both when it labels a noun and when it is the claim of the sentence.}

Complete MR-R49-big and describe a thing three ways -- label a big room, claim that your house is big, and say that you have a big house -- with one adjective doing all three.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[moṭhā]{\mr{मोठा} (moṭhā) — big}

\label{lesson:MR-C49-motha}



\begin{quote}
Forty-eight chapters in you can name a house, put a room in it, say who it belongs to and how to get there. You cannot say one thing about what it is \textbf{like}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mājhyākaḍe ghar āhe}, then \emph{mī mitrālā pāṇī deto}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{मोठा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठा}} — \emph{moṭhā} — \textbf{big, large}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठं} \mr{घर}} — \emph{moṭhaṁ ghar} — \textbf{a big house}
\end{quote}

Start with the ending. The headword is \textbf{\mr{मोठा}}, and the example says \textbf{\mr{मोठं}}. Nothing is wrong: the adjective took the shape of the noun it sits in front of, and \textbf{\mr{घर}} is neuter. The next lesson is about nothing but that.

\textbf{\mr{मोठा}} covers size in every direction — a big house, a big city, a big brother. Where \textbf{\mr{लांब}} measured a distance, this measures a thing.

One warning worth having early. If you know Hindi you will meet \textbf{\mr{मोटा}} (\emph{moṭā}) there and reach for it: it means \textbf{fat}, not \emph{big}, and the two words are a genuine trap between the languages. Marathi's \textbf{\mr{मोठा}} is the neutral, everyday word; nothing about it is about a body.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhā} — big
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhaṁ ghar} — a big house
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{झोपणे}} and then ask for a big room to do it in
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word measures a distance, and which measures a thing? (\textbf{\mr{लांब}}; \textbf{\mr{मोठा}}.) What does the Hindi look-alike \textbf{\mr{मोटा}} mean? (\textbf{Fat} — not the same word.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%A0\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{मोठा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moṭhā · moṭhī · moṭhaṁ]{\mr{मोठा} · \mr{मोठी} · \mr{मोठं} — three endings, one rule}

\label{lesson:MR-C49-adj-agreement}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझा} · \mr{माझी} · \mr{माझं}} from chapter nine. \textbf{\mr{उजवा} · \mr{उजवी} · \mr{उजवं}} from chapter forty-four. The same three endings, twice, and never named.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the adjective takes the gender of its noun}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठा}} \emph{moṭhā} — with a masculine noun
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठी}} \emph{moṭhī} — with a feminine noun
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठं}} \emph{moṭhaṁ} — with a neuter noun
\end{quote}

Marathi has three genders where most European languages have two, and an adjective that ends in \textbf{-\mr{आ}} in its dictionary form changes to match all three. You have owned the machinery since chapter nine; what you did not have was permission to use it on a new word.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठा} \mr{मित्र}} — a big friend (masculine)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठी} \mr{खोली}} — a big room (feminine)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठं} \mr{घर}} — a big house (neuter)
\end{quote}

Say those three aloud and hear that only the last syllable moves. That is what makes the rule cheap: learn one adjective and you have learned three forms, and every \textbf{-\mr{आ}} adjective after this costs you nothing extra.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhā mitra}, \emph{moṭhī khoolī}, \emph{moṭhaṁ ghar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same three endings on \emph{ujvā} — and hear that nothing new happened
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{चालणे}}, and the \emph{chālel} that means \emph{that will do}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which part of the adjective moves? (\textbf{Only the last syllable}.) How many genders does it have to match? (\textbf{Three}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moṭhaṁ … āhe]{\mr{मोठं} … \mr{आहे} — where the adjective stands}

\label{lesson:MR-C49-adj-prenominal}



\begin{quote}
Every adjective this book has shown you — \textbf{\mr{माझा}}, \textbf{\mr{उजवा}}, \textbf{\mr{डावा}}, \textbf{\mr{मोठा}} — has stood in the same place, and nobody has said so.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: in front, always}]
A Marathi adjective goes \textbf{before} its noun and never after it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठं} \mr{घर}} — a big house. Never \emph{\mr{घर} \mr{मोठं}}.
\end{quote}

That is worth saying out loud because it is the opposite of what a Romance language does: Spanish writes \emph{una casa grande} and French \emph{une maison grande}, noun first. English happens to agree with Marathi here, which makes this one of the few places an English speaker can trust the order they already have.

The second position is different, and you have used it since chapter ten without noticing. When the adjective is the whole point of the sentence rather than a label on a noun, it goes at the END, in front of \textbf{\mr{आहे}}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझं} \mr{घर} \mr{मोठं} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{mājhaṁ ghar moṭhaṁ āhe.} — \textbf{my house is big.}
\end{quote}

Two positions, two jobs: \textbf{in front} describes a thing you are naming, \textbf{at the end before \mr{आहे}} makes the description the claim. The ending agrees in both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhaṁ ghar} — the label
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhaṁ ghar moṭhaṁ āhe} — the claim
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mājhyākaḍe moṭhaṁ ghar āhe} — I have a big house
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does an adjective stand when it labels a noun? (\textbf{Before it}.) And when it is the claim of the sentence? (\textbf{At the end, before \mr{आहे}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moṭhā · moṭhī · moṭhaṁ]{Describe a thing for the first time}

\label{lesson:MR-R49-big}



\begin{quote}
One adjective arrived in this chapter and two rules came with it. Name the rules before you use the word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhī khoolī} — and hear the feminine ending
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhaṁ ghar moṭhaṁ āhe}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ḍāvī khoolī} — the left room, with the same machinery
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{सांगणे}} and tell somebody your house is big
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many endings does an \textbf{-\mr{आ}} adjective have, and how many positions? (\textbf{Three endings; two positions}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
